title: Weak shoulders, purple eyelids, and a dry cough
presentation: A 54-year-old woman presents with eight weeks of progressive difficulty climbing stairs and lifting her arms above her head, four weeks of a dry cough with breathlessness on one flight of stairs, and an itchy purplish rash on her eyelids and over her knuckles. Triage: T 37.2 C, HR 92, RR 20, SpO2 93% on air.

stages.label: History
stages.text: The weakness is symmetrical and proximal: she cannot rise from a chair without using her arms and cannot comb her hair. Grip, walking on flat ground, and sensation are normal. No double vision, no fluctuation through the day, no fasciculations. For two weeks solids have been sticking in her throat and she has coughed once or twice while eating. The rash began on the upper eyelids, then scaly red bumps appeared over the knuckles; there is redness over her upper chest and shoulders that worsens in the sun. No Raynaud's, no joint swelling, no fever. She has lost 2 kg. Past history: hypothyroidism on a stable dose of levothyroxine (TSH 2.1 three months ago). No statin or other new medication. Never smoked. Mammogram two years ago and cervical smear one year ago were normal; she has never had a colonoscopy. No family history of neuromuscular disease.
stages.prompt: What is your differential for subacute proximal weakness with a rash, and what tests do you want first?
stages.learner_goal: Name an inflammatory myopathy, specifically dermatomyositis, and order creatine kinase while keeping the mimics (statin, thyroid, inclusion body myositis, neuromuscular junction) in view.

stages.label: Exam
stages.text: Violaceous erythema of both upper eyelids with periorbital oedema (heliotrope rash). Flat-topped violaceous papules over the MCP and PIP joints (Gottron's papules). Periungual erythema with ragged cuticles and dilated nailfold capillary loops. Confluent erythema over the anterior chest (V sign) and across the shoulders and upper back (shawl sign). No mechanic's hands, no skin ulceration, no calcinosis. Power: neck flexion 4/5, shoulder abduction 3+/5, hip flexion 3+/5, distal power 5/5. Reflexes and sensation normal. No fatigability on sustained upgaze. Chest: fine, dry, end-inspiratory crackles at both bases. SpO2 93% at rest, falling to 88% after walking the corridor. Heart sounds normal, no raised JVP. No lymphadenopathy, breast and abdominal examination normal.
stages.prompt: Commit to your leading diagnosis. What explains her hypoxaemia and crackles, and how will you characterise it? Which tests confirm the muscle disease?
stages.learner_goal: Diagnose dermatomyositis clinically, suspect interstitial lung disease, and order HRCT with full pulmonary function tests plus CK, EMG or MRI, myositis antibodies, and a swallow assessment.

available_tests.liver enzymes: ALT 142, AST 165, LDH 540 U/L (consistent with muscle source)
available_tests.myositis antibody panel: Myositis-specific antibodies (anti-Jo-1, PL-7, PL-12, EJ, OJ, MDA5, TIF1-gamma, NXP2, Mi-2, SAE, SRP, HMGCR) all negative; anti-Ro52 positive
available_tests.emg: EMG: short-duration, low-amplitude polyphasic motor unit potentials with early recruitment, fibrillation potentials and positive sharp waves in proximal muscles (irritable myopathy); nerve conduction normal
available_tests.mri thighs: MRI thighs: symmetrical T2/STIR oedema in quadriceps and adductors with fascial oedema, no fatty replacement
available_tests.muscle biopsy: Deltoid biopsy: perifascicular atrophy, perimysial and perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, MHC class I upregulation; consistent with dermatomyositis
available_tests.skin biopsy: Skin biopsy of a Gottron's papule: interface dermatitis with dermal mucin
available_tests.chest x-ray: Bilateral lower-zone reticular shadowing, normal heart size
available_tests.hrct chest: HRCT: bilateral, lower-lobe-predominant ground-glass opacity with fine reticulation and traction bronchiectasis, relative subpleural sparing, no honeycombing; pattern consistent with non-specific interstitial pneumonia (NSIP)
available_tests.pulmonary function tests: FVC 62% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.85, TLC 65% predicted, DLCO 48% predicted
available_tests.echocardiogram: Normal biventricular function, estimated PA pressure normal
available_tests.videofluoroscopic swallow: Mild pharyngeal residue with delayed swallow initiation; no frank aspiration

stages.label: Results
stages.text: CK 4,850 U/L, aldolase raised, ALT/AST and LDH raised in proportion; troponin I normal. TSH 2.3. ANA 1:320 speckled. Myositis-specific antibody panel negative; anti-Ro52 positive. EMG: irritable myopathy. MRI thighs: symmetrical muscle and fascial oedema. HRCT chest: lower-lobe ground-glass with reticulation and traction bronchiectasis, NSIP pattern, no honeycombing. PFTs: FVC 62%, DLCO 48%. Echocardiogram normal. Videofluoroscopy: pharyngeal weakness without frank aspiration. Deltoid biopsy: perifascicular atrophy with perivascular inflammation.
stages.prompt: The muscle and lung disease are now defined. There is one more thing you must look for in a 54-year-old with new dermatomyositis. What is it, how hard should you look in her specifically, and what in her story raises or lowers that risk?
stages.learner_goal: Recognise dermatomyositis as a paraneoplastic phenomenon and plan a risk-stratified malignancy screen, noting that age over 40, dermatomyositis subtype, and dysphagia raise risk while ILD and the absence of anti-TIF1-gamma lower it.

stages.label: Malignancy screen
stages.text: CT chest, abdomen, and pelvis with contrast: interstitial changes as on HRCT, no mass, no lymphadenopathy, normal ovaries and adnexa. Mammography and breast ultrasound normal. Transvaginal ultrasound normal; CA-125 normal. Faecal immunochemical test negative; colonoscopy booked. Serum and urine protein electrophoresis normal. No cancer identified at baseline.
stages.prompt: Final diagnosis and treatment plan for muscle, skin, lung, and swallow. What steroid-sparing agent and why, what do you do about the dysphagia, and what is your screening plan from here?
stages.learner_goal: Start high-dose glucocorticoids with an immunosuppressant chosen for the lung disease, plan IVIG for dysphagia if needed, and commit to repeat cancer screening over the next three years.

diagnosis: Dermatomyositis with interstitial lung disease (NSIP pattern)
key_clues: Symmetrical proximal weakness with preserved sensation and reflexes
Heliotrope rash, Gottron's papules, V and shawl signs, nailfold capillary changes: pathognomonic skin findings
CK 4,850 with irritable myopathy on EMG and muscle oedema on MRI
Perifascicular atrophy on biopsy, the histological signature of dermatomyositis
Bibasal velcro crackles, exertional desaturation, NSIP pattern on HRCT with restrictive PFTs and DLCO 48%
Anti-Ro52 positivity, associated with myositis-related ILD
Age over 40, dermatomyositis subtype, and dysphagia: features that raise cancer risk

distractors.name: Statin-associated or anti-HMGCR necrotising myopathy
distractors.why_not: She takes no statin, anti-HMGCR is negative, and necrotising myopathy has no rash.

distractors.name: Hypothyroid myopathy
distractors.why_not: TSH is 2.3 on a stable levothyroxine dose; hypothyroid myopathy does not produce Gottron's papules or EMG irritability of this degree.

distractors.name: Inclusion body myositis
distractors.why_not: IBM is slowly progressive, asymmetric, favours finger flexors and quadriceps, has a modest CK, and has no rash.

distractors.name: Antisynthetase syndrome
distractors.why_not: A reasonable thought given ILD, but all antisynthetase antibodies are negative and she has no mechanic's hands, Raynaud's, fever, or arthritis.

distractors.name: Systemic lupus erythematosus
distractors.why_not: ANA is positive but the rash is over the knuckles (lupus spares them), there are no cytopenias, serositis, or nephritis, and the CK and biopsy define a primary myositis.

distractors.name: Myasthenia gravis
distractors.why_not: No fatigability or ocular involvement, reflexes normal, and a CK of 4,850 with a myopathic EMG points to muscle, not the neuromuscular junction.

distractors.name: Aspiration pneumonitis or heart failure as the cause of crackles
distractors.why_not: Videofluoroscopy shows no aspiration, the echocardiogram is normal, and HRCT shows a bilateral NSIP pattern with restrictive physiology and low DLCO.

rubric.description: Names dermatomyositis or an inflammatory myopathy at the history stage
rubric.concept: Subacute symmetrical proximal weakness with a heliotrope or knuckle rash is dermatomyositis

rubric.description: Orders creatine kinase and a confirmatory muscle test (EMG, MRI, or biopsy)
rubric.concept: CK first; EMG or MRI localises and guides biopsy; biopsy is needed when the rash or antibodies are not diagnostic

rubric.description: Names the pathognomonic skin findings (heliotrope, Gottron's, shawl or V sign, nailfold changes)
rubric.concept: Heliotrope rash and Gottron's papules are specific enough to make the diagnosis clinically

rubric.description: Suspects interstitial lung disease and orders HRCT with pulmonary function tests including DLCO
rubric.concept: Every new myositis patient gets HRCT and PFTs with DLCO at baseline; lung disease drives mortality

rubric.description: Sends a myositis-specific antibody panel and uses it to stratify lung and cancer risk
rubric.concept: Myositis antibodies define phenotype: anti-MDA5 means rapidly progressive ILD, anti-TIF1-gamma and anti-NXP2 mean cancer, antisynthetase means ILD with arthritis and mechanic's hands

rubric.description: Raises the possibility of an underlying malignancy and plans a screen
rubric.concept: Adult dermatomyositis carries a 15-25% cancer risk, highest in the three years around diagnosis; screen at diagnosis and stratify intensity by risk

rubric.description: Final diagnosis is dermatomyositis (ideally with ILD named)
Starts glucocorticoids with a steroid-sparing immunosuppressant suited to ILD (mycophenolate, azathioprine, tacrolimus, or rituximab), or IVIG for dysphagia
rubric.concept: Glucocorticoids plus a steroid-sparing agent from the start; with ILD prefer mycophenolate, azathioprine, or a calcineurin inhibitor over methotrexate; IVIG for dysphagia and refractory skin or muscle disease

rubric.description: Commits to repeated cancer screening over the next three years, or to pulmonary follow-up with serial PFTs
rubric.concept: Cancer risk persists for about three years after diagnosis, so screening is repeated; lung function is tracked with serial PFTs

management_summary: Dermatomyositis with NSIP-pattern interstitial lung disease, pharyngeal dysphagia, and no cancer found at baseline. Start prednisolone 1 mg/kg (consider three days of intravenous methylprednisolone given FVC 62% and DLCO 48%) together with a steroid-sparing agent from day one; mycophenolate mofetil 2-3 g/day is the usual choice when the lung is involved, with tacrolimus or rituximab for progression, and cyclophosphamide reserved for rapidly progressive disease. Avoid methotrexate as first choice with significant ILD. Add IVIG early for the dysphagia (and for refractory skin or muscle disease); until the swallow improves, modified-consistency diet and speech and language review, with aspiration precautions. Sun protection, topical steroids, and hydroxychloroquine for the skin (watch for the drug rash that is more common in dermatomyositis). Physiotherapy from the start, bone protection, Pneumocystis prophylaxis while on high-dose steroids. Monitor CK, strength, FVC and DLCO every three months initially. Because she has multiple high-risk features (dermatomyositis subtype, age over 40, dysphagia), complete the colonoscopy and repeat enhanced cancer screening (CT chest, abdomen and pelvis, breast and gynaecological screening) annually for three years, with a low threshold for PET-CT if symptoms arise.
teaching_points: Proximal weakness plus a heliotrope rash or Gottron's papules is dermatomyositis; CK, EMG or MRI, and antibodies support it, and biopsy is needed mainly when the rash is absent, the antibodies are negative, or the picture is atypical. Troponin I, not troponin T, tells you whether the heart is involved, because regenerating skeletal muscle releases troponin T.

Every new myositis patient gets a baseline HRCT and full PFTs with DLCO, and a swallow assessment if there is any dysphagia. Lung disease, not muscle, is what kills; anti-MDA5-positive patients can progress to respiratory failure in weeks and need urgent combination immunosuppression.

Adult dermatomyositis is paraneoplastic until a screen says otherwise: roughly one in five has a cancer within three years of diagnosis. Stratify by risk: dermatomyositis subtype, age over 40, dysphagia, cutaneous necrosis, and anti-TIF1-gamma or anti-NXP2 push towards enhanced screening with CT chest, abdomen and pelvis and sex-specific tests, repeated over three years; ILD, Raynaud's, arthritis, and antisynthetase or anti-MDA5 antibodies are associated with lower risk.

Treat with glucocorticoids plus a steroid-sparing agent from the start, and choose the agent for the organ at stake: mycophenolate, azathioprine, or a calcineurin inhibitor when the lung is involved, with IVIG for dysphagia and refractory disease (ProDERM).
